indian-startups-bd47009bf3.headline: Pune-based deeptech startup Aeron Systems raises Rs 45 crore in pre-Series B funding
indian-startups-bd47009bf3.fulltext:
Pune-based deeptech startup Aeron Systems has raised Rs 45 crore ($4.7 million) in a pre-Series B funding round jointly led by Riverwalk Holdings and MGF-Kavachh (MountTech Growth Fund).
The startup said the funding will be used to expand manufacturing capacity for advanced inertial navigation systems, accelerate research and development, support product development and meet customer demand.
It also plans to use the investment to expand its presence in international markets.
Founded in 2008 by Ashvani Shukla and Abhijeet Bokil, Aeron develops navigation, weather sensing and monitoring technologies for aerospace, defence and industrial applications.
Its product portfolio includes inertial navigation systems, air data computers, weather and environmental sensing systems, flight test instrumentation, avionics and resilient Positioning, Navigation and Timing technologies.
The systems are designed for platforms including aircraft, helicopters, unmanned vehicles, missiles, armoured vehicles and naval platforms.
According to the startup, its technologies are used by organisations including Hindustan Aeronautics Limited, Bharat Electronics Limited, the Defence Research and Development Organisation, the Indian Army and the Indian Navy.
Ashvani Shukla, co-founder and CEO of Aeron Systems, said the investment marked an important stage in the company's development.
“This investment marks an important milestone for Aeron Systems as we enter our next phase of growth. We are delighted to partner with investors who share our long-term vision of building globally competitive technologies from India while supporting the country's strategic and technological self-reliance,” he said.
Co-founder and managing director Abhijeet Bokil said the funding would support Aeron's international expansion while strengthening its manufacturing capabilities.
He said the company aimed to take its experience in aerospace and renewable energy, as well as its sensing and navigation technologies, to more overseas customers.
R.K.S. Bhadauria, a retired Air Chief Marshal and chairman of the Strategy and Oversight Board at MGF-Kavachh, said the investment reflected confidence in Aeron's technology and leadership.
“Modern defence platforms require technologies that can continue to operate reliably in contested environments. Aeron has built an impressive portfolio of indigenous capabilities across aerospace sensing and navigation, backed by strong engineering expertise and proven execution,” he said.
Raj Sethia, founder and managing partner at MGF-Kavachh, described Aeron as a “sovereign-technology company” with the potential to strengthen India's strategic technology ecosystem.
Riverwalk Holdings principal Abhishek Singh said the company saw opportunities in two areas: inertial navigation for environments where satellite-navigation signals are denied, spoofed or jammed, and hardware and software used in utility-scale solar projects.
“Aeron Systems is one of the most unique companies being built out of India,” Singh said, adding that Riverwalk was backing the company's international ambitions.
Alongside its aerospace and defence operations, Aeron develops weather monitoring and related hardware and software technologies for renewable-energy applications, including utility-scale solar projects.
The new funding will support its next phase of manufacturing, product development and international expansion, it said.

india-1a79e05697.headline: Nepal’s Floods Upset Its China-India Balancing Act - The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine
india-1a79e05697.source: The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine
india-1a79e05697.fulltext:
Nepal’s recent floods, which have killed at least 1,280 people while over 5,600 are still missing as of this writing, rank among the country’s worst natural disasters. Preliminary estimates put economic losses at $2.56 billion. But the disaster’s consequences will extend far beyond the immediate human and economic toll.
It has also undermined the efforts of successive post-2015 governments to achieve more geopolitical balance, largely through the development of new transport, trade and transit facilities with China.
As a landlocked country wedged between India and China, Nepal has long sought to preserve its strategic autonomy by balancing the influence of its two neighbors.
For a variety of reasons, India, which surrounds the country on three sides, has blockaded its open border with Nepal three times since 1969 — most recently in 2015. That year, Nepal promulgated a new constitution that had failed to address India’s concerns. At other times, New Delhi has openly meddled in Nepali politics.
To reduce that vulnerability to Indian pressure, Nepali rulers have felt the need to increase engagement with China, the northern neighbor.
After the 2015 blockade, the then-K.P. Sharma Oli government signed a slew of agreements with China to establish new trade and transit links. As part of the process, a significant investment was made to upgrade the Kerung border point (known as Gyirong on the Chinese side) into an all-weather international crossing. Much of China-Nepal trade has gradually shifted to Kerung from Tatopani, the previous main artery of bilateral trade that was badly damaged by the 2015 earthquakes.
Unfortunately, the recent floods literally washed away much of the investment around Kerung. There is not even a trace of the customs buildings and customs yards — on either side of the border.
After the flooding of the Kerung border, China has also shut down Tatopani, citing possible landslides on the Nepali side. (Beijing has also long been wary of the possible use of the Tatopani route by “Free Tibet” activists.) All cross-border traffic has been diverted to Korala, the third international border crossing between Nepal and China. But Korala is not an easy crossing, nor is there much in terms of cross-border trade infrastructure. Besides these three, the three other designated points for Nepal-China trade are minuscule and limited to handling local trade.
In the big picture, Nepal’s trade with China, which was already limited, will be further restricted after the floods.
India is Nepal’s largest trade partner, with China coming in at a distant second. The floods will exacerbate an already troubling imbalance. But Kathmandu’s options are limited. Rebuilding Kerung or upgrading Korala to handle more traffic will require a lot of time and money. Shipping goods from China is an option, but a costly one. The country’s dependence on India will thus further increase. Besides the prospect of some Indian goods replacing Chinese ones in Nepali markets, Nepal will now have to use Indian ports to import even vital supplies from China.
With the floods knocking out around 10 percent of Nepal’s electricity-generation capacity, the energy dependence on India could go up too.
The Rasuwa floods will strengthen the argument that geography leaves Nepal with no realistic substitute for India as its principal commercial and transit partner, with China serving mainly as a supplementary option. And as India’s commercial clout increases in Nepal, so will its strategic sway. Nepal, after all, shares a long, flat open border with India and the two countries are bound together by cultural and family ties.
Nepali Prime Minister Balen Shah had already complicated Nepal’s external relations with his unconventional approach, initially avoiding individual meetings with foreign envoys and senior visiting officials. Beijing, with whom Nepal will now have to work closely to rebuild damaged infrastructure along the border, was particularly displeased at what it saw as the Nepal government’s repeated failures to uphold the “One China” policy.
Yet rebuilding Nepal’s northern connectivity could itself have geopolitical consequences. Kathmandu will need Chinese technical and financial assistance to restore damaged border infrastructure. China will also be averse to involving other countries in reconstruction in the sensitive region. The floods could therefore produce a peculiar form of dual dependence: greater reliance on India for immediate trade and transit, even as Nepal turns to China to rebuild the infrastructure needed to reduce that very reliance.
For the 36-year-old Nepali prime minister, this creates a separate political dilemma. Shah will have to rely more on India for trade and connectivity while also being under pressure to maintain a safe distance from New Delhi — in keeping with the wishes of core nationalist constituencies.
The mountainous trade routes to China have long been vulnerable to landslides and earthquakes, limiting the northern neighbor’s viability as a trade and transit alternative to India. The recent disaster has highlighted this weakness like never before.
The floods will not change Nepal’s need to balance India and China. What they will change is the feasibility of one crucial component of that strategy.

other-interests-d150db9460.headline: Neuromodulation for restoring and amplifying brain function
other-interests-d150db9460.fulltext:
Abstract
Neuromodulation aims to improve brain function by altering neural activity. While many rehabilitation strategies seek to restore normal, healthy-like dynamics, some adopt a complementary strategy, using neuromodulation to strengthen repurposed processes that support function. Here we formalize these approaches as ‘restorative normalization’ (RN) and ‘compensatory amplification’ (CA), respectively. Drawing on cognitive neurophysiology, we evaluate the following four factors that enable CA to be effective: multiple realizability, multiscale neuroplasticity, precision readiness and activity selectivity. We analyze the interplay between RN and CA across clinical goals, such as stroke rehabilitation, and identify opportunities in neurodegeneration, psychiatry and aging where CA could delay decline, facilitate remission or increase neural processing capacity. We propose that positioning CA alongside RN as a core design principle can sharpen target selection, guide stratified treatments and translate known compensatory signatures into testable neuromodulation protocols.

longform-b3f4caaad6.headline: Your Smartwatch May Not be as Smart as You Think it is
longform-b3f4caaad6.fulltext:
Smartwatches have soared in popularity in recent years, and now roughly 30-40 percent of American adults own one of them. More than serving as just a timepiece or a second screen for notifications, these watches promise to monitor a growing number of health metrics—from blood pressure to sweat loss. But how accurate are they really?
Kinesiologists from the University of Michigan recently published a new framework to help users understand what, exactly, smartwatches are measuring.
Read more: “The Pitfalls of AI Health Coaches”
If you take a peek under the hood of your average smartwatch, you’ll find a suite of sensors, including an accelerometer, a gyroscope, GPS, and a photoplethysmogram (or PPG, which uses light to detect blood volume). These sensors collect raw data (acceleration, angular velocity, location, and optical signal data), and the good news is, they’re pretty accurate.
But this data is just the input to the smartwatch, what users (and would-be consumers) are most interested in are the outputs. According to the researchers, this is where things get fuzzy. That’s because the signal provided by the raw data gets filtered through a layer of proprietary algorithms that churn out metrics like heart rate, physical activity, sleep duration, etc. The more recent the model, the more exotic the metric (i.e., water loss during exercise).
According to the team, the farther from the sensory data the outputs are, the less accurate they are. For example, metrics like heart rate, step count, and outdoor pace are much more reliable than metrics like calories burned, sleep stages, blood glucose, and hydration loss. These “metrics” are more like estimates.
“People shouldn’t take these metrics at face value,” study author Adam Lepley said in a statement. “In many cases, these devices are better suited to tracking trends over time, rather than as precise laboratory measurements.”
And that’s an important point. While these more exotic metrics may not represent a one-to-one agreement with lab-grade measures, they’re still useful for tracking your own progress over time. (Of course, the algorithms that generate the metrics are proprietary so if you switch brands they’re not likely to match.) The researchers also stress that any higher level recommendations from your devices, like exercise recovery time, should be taken with a grain of salt.
In other words, listen to your body. It might be smarter than your watch.

longform-addc2a8883.headline: The Longreads Questionnaire, Featuring Jon Ronson
longform-addc2a8883.fulltext:
“I do unashamedly want to write page-turners,” Jon Ronson told The New Yorker in an interview. “I can never understand why most nonfiction books have such limited creative ambitions.” Ronson, who is “not a thrill-seeker,” then recounts fearing for his life while being pursued by members of a secretive political gathering—a chase that found its way into Them: Adventures with Extremists, his 2001 breakthrough book. Thrills have a way of finding Ronson, either through active pursuit or some subtler means of revelation. The Men Who Stare At Goats begins with a US Army general who attempts to walk through walls, repeatedly smacking into them. In the opening of The Psychopath Test, a neurologist hands Ronson a baffling package, copies of which have been anonymously mailed to academics throughout the world. The pages turn themselves.
Ronson’s latest, The Castle, earned a starred review from Publisher’s Weekly, which praised the book as “a blockbuster portrait of men gone mad” and Ronson’s style as “intuitive but rigorous.” His podcast, Things Fell Apart, was recently renewed for a third season, in which Ronson will shift focus from American culture wars to individual battles against institutions. He once told The Guardian, “I get called faux-naïf all the time. But I honestly think I am just genuinely naive.” It’s an observation that reminds me of Joan Didion’s own famous self-assessment: that she was “so physically small, so temperamentally unobtrusive . . . that people tend to forget that my presence runs counter to their best interests.” Ronson is warmer than that, but his access is no less astonishing. Time and again, someone allows him to get very close—closer, perhaps, than they might be aware of. Each of Ronson’s books is a testament to his depth of inquiry, his proximity to the surprising, and his conviction that a good narrative should be propulsive.
—Brendan Fitzgerald
Where did you grow up?
Cardiff, Wales. In a suburb called Lisvane.
What places feel like home?
London, for sure. As a child, when we’d visit my grandparents, I’d sneak away and jump on a bus and just get lost in the City. Even when it wasn’t home, it felt like home. Eventually I lived there for decades, loving especially Soho and Islington. I also love our tiny town in the Hudson Valley. We’ve lived here since 2019.
Other than family members, who or what has shaped you the most?
As a teenager, watching Nick Broomfield documentaries and reading the great nonfiction adventurers from the ’60s and ’70s like Hunter S. Thompson and PJ O’Rourke and the writers featured in Tom Wolfe’s The New Journalism. And when I started in journalism, the editors who first gave me a break: Ian Parker, Chris Heath, Deborah Orr, Ian Katz.
What is your favorite time of day?
Early morning. I make a coffee and for the first few hours my brain is at its best and I can write a lot.
What are you really good at?
Narrative nonfiction. If I go off on some journey, I know exactly how to make it work. It’s the only thing I’m good at.
What’s the best gift you’ve ever received?
Recently the BBC gave me a subscription to Descript, a text-based audio editing program. It’s a dream gift for a detail-oriented storyteller. I can finally do the audio editing myself. I sit there for hours.
Describe your favorite meal.
I guess some kind of salad with lots of fruit and vegetables and a good dressing. You can’t beat Greek dressing.
Sound or silence? (And if sound, what sound?)
Silence! I can’t believe how great the silence is here in the Hudson Valley. There’s something very comforting about knowing it won’t end. They’ll never turn this country lane into a big road.
Where do you do your best thinking?
When I’m out on a story, in some strange place, gathering material. I just instinctively know what’ll work, what the best moments are. Fiction people can do that in their imaginations. I can’t. But when I’m out on a story, I just know.
What journey—physical, creative, intellectual, or otherwise—has meant the most to you?
The journey of leaving Cardiff and moving to London when I was 18. I felt like finally my life could begin.
Where do you like to read?
I listen to audiobooks when I’m out walking.
What’s the last rabbit hole you disappeared into?
The Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC). I went to the cage match on the White House South Lawn for GQ, because it was theme-adjacent to my new book The Castle. So I watched all manner of fighter interviews and UFC super-fan videos for that.
Name three publications you enjoy reading these days.
The New Yorker, The Guardian, The New York Times.
What’s one longread that you can’t stop thinking about?
“Andrew Tate’s Empire Of Abuse” was the last one I listened to from beginning to end.
What was the last book you read?
Shakespeare: The World as Stage by Bill Bryson. I listen to it over and over to get to sleep. So I still don’t know how he dies.
What piece of nonfiction are you most proud of writing?
Every book I’ve written has chapters I’m equally proud of: sneaking into Bohemian Grove with Alex Jones and getting chased by the Bilderberg Group in Them, the goat staring in The Men Who Stare At Goats, pretty much all of The Psychopath Test, much of Lost at Sea, Justine Sacco in So You’ve Been Publicly Shamed. The Castle feels really good. I felt very confident writing it, mixing up tones and styles in a way I don’t think I could have managed before.
What’s your most reliable way to get creatively unstuck?
Just wandering around Reddit can be good. The whole world is somewhere on Reddit. And if you don’t find your next story, it might still unlock some part of your brain.
Who’s a writer you turn to when you need some inspiration?
Kurt Vonnegut, for his brevity and his clashes between comedy and horror.
What words do you overuse?
It used to be “There was a silence” but I’ve cured myself of that, thank God.
What’s your favorite guilty pleasure?
I don’t know if this counts, but every book I read for pleasure is a celebrity memoir, mostly musicians and actors. Cher. Anthony Hopkins. Bruce Springsteen. I LOVED the English actor Kathy Burke’s one, A Mind Of My Own. Right now it’s Johnny Marr.
What superpower would you like to have?
I think I’d like to be able to shoot fire out of my hands. No. Teleportation through space and time.
What animal or nonhuman being do you most identify with?
I really identified with my dog, Floppy—how he wanted to be around people but didn’t want to interact with them.
If you have a free solitary hour in your day, what do you typically do?
Run or walk.
What five items would you place in a time capsule?
Talking Heads’ Stop Making Sense. The Pitt. Succession. All of NPR’s Tiny Desk Concerts, especially Doechii, Sierra Ferrell, and Chappell Roan. Bruce Springsteen’s 1979 No Nukes concert video. Huh, it’s almost all music. I guess that’s the stuff we should remember. People being their best.
What does your writing space look like?
Jon Ronson’s nonfiction books include So You’ve Been Publicly Shamed, The Psychopath Test, Them: Adventures with Extremists, Lost at Sea, and The Men Who Stare At Goats. They have all been international and/or New York Times bestsellers and have been translated into more than 30 languages. His latest book, The Castle, is now available.
